Large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong performance in long-horizon tasks that require planning, tool use, and interaction with external environments. However, most existing benchmarks implicitly assume a monolingual setting, where the entire execution process, including reasoning, tool invocation, and output generation, is conducted within a single language. In contrast, real-world applications often involve multilingual inputs and outputs within a unified workflow, yet the interaction between multilinguality and agentic execution remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce PolyWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on multilingual long-horizon workplace workflows. PolyWorkBench consists of 67 tasks across five domains, including commerce, knowledge work, legal analysis, localization, and manufacturing, where agents must process heterogeneous multilingual inputs, perform iterative reasoning, invoke external tools, and produce structured outputs. To enable comprehensive evaluation, we propose a hybrid framework that combines structural grading, executable verification, and LLM-based semantic assessment. This design allows us to capture both functional correctness and linguistic consistency across complex workflows. Empirical results show that state-of-the-art LLM agents suffer significant performance degradation in multilingual workflow settings compared to monolingual counterparts. Our analysis suggests that multilinguality introduces

compounding effects across reasoning and execution steps, highlighting the importance of jointly modeling language variation and procedural decision-making in agent evaluation. Date:July 7, 2026 Correspondence:Hongliang Li atsuperhanslerli@gmail.com, Kaiyu Huang atkyhuang@bjtu.edu.cn

Recent advances in large language model (LLM) agents have enabled substantial progress in solving complex long-horizon tasks that require planning, tool use, and interaction with external environments. A growing line of work has introduced benchmarks that simulate realistic workflows in web environments, software engineering tasks, and office applications, including SWE-bench Jimenez et al. (2024), WebArena Zhou et al. (2024), OSWorld Xie et al. (2024), and more recent workflow-oriented benchmarks such as OdysseyBench Wang et al. (2025) and CoffeeBench Sugiura et al. (2026). These benchmarks collectively emphasize sequential decision-making and extended interaction horizons, revealing that current agents still struggle with sustained execution and robust tool coordination. Despite these advances, most existing evaluation settings implicitly assume that the entire agentic process operates within a single linguistic regime. Task instructions, intermediate reasoning, tool interactions, and final outputs are typically expressed in English, with multilinguality either absent or reduced to surface-level translation. This assumption simplifies the evaluation pipeline but overlooks an important characteristic of real-world deployments, where agents must operate over heterogeneous linguistic inputs and outputs within a single coherent workflow. In parallel, multilingual NLP research has extensively studied cross-lingual transfer and multilingual generalization, as reflected in benchmarks such as XGLUE Liang et al. (2020), M-MMLU Lai et al. (2023),
and MGSM Shi et al. (2022). These studies demonstrate that language variation significantly affects model 1

performance, particularly under low-resource or cross-lingual transfer conditions. However, such evaluations are predominantly confined to isolated prediction tasks, where each instance is independent and does not involve multi-step interaction or tool-based execution. A key limitation of these two research directions is that they treatmultilingualityandagentic reasoningas orthogonal dimensions. In multilingual benchmarks, language variation is studied in static settings without execution dynamics. In agent benchmarks, execution complexity is studied under monolingual assumptions. As a result, an important question remains underexplored: how language variation affects the stability of reasoning and decision-making trajectories in long-horizon agent workflows. We argue that multilinguality should not be viewed as a property of inputs or outputs alone, but as a factor that influences the entire execution trajectory of an agent. In realistic workplace scenarios, agents must interpret instructions in one language, retrieve or transform information in another language, and produce structured artifacts in potentially different target languages. This introduces a form of cross-lingual trajectory coupling, where errors may propagate across reasoning, tool use, and generation stages in ways that are not captured by existing evaluation paradigms. To study this phenomenon, we introducePolyWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on multilingual long-horizon workplace workflows. PolyWorkBench consists of 67 tasks spanning five domains,

including commerce, knowledge work, legal analysis, localization, and manufacturing. Each task requires agents to process heterogeneous inputs such as documents, tables, and multilingual resources, perform iterative reasoning, invoke external tools, and generate structured outputs. A central design principle of PolyWorkBench is that language variation is embedded into the execution process rather than treated as an auxiliary attribute of input data. Agents must maintain semantic consistency across languages throughout intermediate reasoning steps and final output generation. This setting exposes failure modes that arise specifically from the interaction between cross-lingual transfer and multi-step execution, which are not observable in either standard multilingual benchmarks or monolingual agent benchmarks. We further propose a hybrid evaluation framework combining structural grading, executable verification, and LLM-based semantic assessment, enabling robust evaluation of both functional correctness and linguistic consistency. Empirical results show that state-of-the-art LLM agents experience substantial degradation in multilingual workflow settings, even when they perform strongly on monolingual long-horizon benchmarks. Our analysis suggests that multilinguality introduces compounding effects across execution trajectories, affecting not only comprehension but also planning stability and tool-use reliability. These findings indicate that future agent evaluation should jointly consider language variation and procedural execution, rather than treating them as

Agent Benchmarks.The emergence of large language models has driven the development of increasingly realistic benchmarks for evaluating autonomous agents. Early efforts, such as AgentBench Liu et al. (2024), established unified evaluation across multiple interactive environments, demonstrating the feasibility of assessing LLMs beyond static language understanding tasks. Subsequent benchmarks expanded evaluation to more realistic settings, including web navigation (WebArena Zhou et al. (2024)), open-world assistant tasks (GAIA Mialon et al. (2024)), and desktop computer operation (OSWorld Xie et al. (2024)). Domain-specific benchmarks, such as SWE-bench Jimenez et al. (2024), MLE-bench Chan et al. (2025), andτ-bench Yao et al. (2024), further evaluate agents in professional software engineering and tool-use scenarios. More recent workflow-oriented benchmarks, including Claw-Eval Ye et al. (2026), Claw-Eval-Live Li et al. (2026), WildClawBench Ding et al. (2026), and ClawMark Meng et al. (2026), emphasize persistent environments, evolving workflows, and trustworthy evaluation for long-horizon agents. Compared with these benchmarks, PolyWorkBench focuses on multilingual enterprise workplace tasks that require cross-lingual reasoning, heterogeneous document understanding, and end-to-end workflow execution across diverse professional domains. More recent benchmarks have shifted toward realistic task settings. MAPS Hofman et al. (2026) and MIRAGE- Bench Thakur et al. (2025) evaluate multilingual agents on complex multi-step tasks that require planning, tool use, and cross-lingual reasoning. Other task-oriented benchmarks, including SpreadsheetBench Ma et al. (2024), OfficeBench Wang et al. (2024), and LongDoc or RAGBench Friel et al. (2024), further investigate agents’ abilities to process structured documents, long-context information, and retrieval-intensive workflows. While these benchmarks significantly broaden multilingual and task-oriented evaluation, they typically focus on individual capabilities, specific application domains, or limited interaction settings. In contrast, PolyWorkBench integrates multilingual understanding, heterogeneous document processing, long-horizon reasoning, and structured output generation into unified end-to-end tasks spanning diverse real-world scenarios. Benchmark Evaluation and LLM-as-a-Judge.As benchmarks become more open-ended, evaluation has shifted

from rule-based metrics toward model-based and preference-driven assessment. Traditional metrics such as exact match are often insufficient for generative and multi-turn tasks. LLM-as-a-judge has therefore emerged as a scalable paradigm, where strong language models approximate human evaluation. Representative systems such as MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena Zheng et al. (2023) show that GPT-4-level models can achieve high agreement with human judgments while enabling large-scale evaluation of openended outputs. Similarly, AlpacaEval Li et al. (2023) uses pairwise ranking to compare instruction-following performance efficiently across models. However, prior work has identified limitations including position bias, verbosity bias, and sensitivity to prompting and model configuration Zheng et al. (2023). These issues raise concerns about robustness, particularly in complex or long-horizon evaluation settings. Overall, while LLM-as-a-judge is practical and scalable, reliable evaluation of multilingual and multi-step agent workflows remains an open challenge. 3

PolyWorkBench evaluates LLM agents on realistic long-horizon workplace tasks. Unlike prior benchmarks that isolate a single capability such as reasoning or tool use, it targets complete task execution in professional scenarios that require multilingual understanding, iterative reasoning, external tool use, and structured artefact generation. The benchmark comprises 67 tasks across five workplace domains—Commerce (COM), Knowledge (KNW), Legal (LEG), Localization (LOC), and Manufacturing (MFG)—and covers ten languages. Each task is an end-to-end workflow with executable outputs rather than a single-turn question.

Each task is a complete business workflow: the agent receives an instruction with supporting materials— documents, spreadsheets, logs, contracts, or multilingual resources—and must deliver artefacts that satisfy predefined requirements. Tasks require long-horizon reasoning over multiple intermediate steps rather than direct answer generation. Depending on the scenario, the agent must retrieve information from heterogeneous inputs, perform multilingual comprehension and translation, invoke external tools, integrate intermediate results, and produce structured outputs such as reports, spreadsheets, summaries, legal documents, localization artefacts, or operational analyses. The five domains cover complementary enterprise workflows.Commercefocuses on cross-border operations, pricing, logistics, taxation, and marketplace management.Knowledgefocuses on information synthesis, technical reporting, patent analysis, and multilingual fact verification.Legalfocuses on compliance analysis, contract review, regulatory comparison, and legal document drafting.Localizationfocuses on multilingual adaptation of software, documentation, subtitles, and marketing material.Manufacturingfocuses on quality management, production reporting, maintenance, safety auditing, and supply-chain analysis.

Every task in PolyWorkBench is authored by hand rather than crawled or generated in bulk. We follow a three-stage curation pipeline.(i) Source materials.For each scenario a domain-familiar annotator collects native-language artefacts that match the target workflow: Japanese receipts and freight invoices for Commerce, Korean SRE incident logs and Chinese sensor traces for Manufacturing, German framework agreements and Spanish evidence chains for Legal, native-language product strings and marketing copy for Localization, and Russian/Vietnamese market research memos for Knowledge. Public documents (regulatory notices, template contracts, published patents) are used verbatim; proprietary-style artefacts (internal reports, shift handovers) are drafted from scratch in the target language by the same annotator. Machine translation is never used to produce a source-language file.(ii) Instruction and reference authoring.The annotator writes the instruction in one of the ten target languages and, in parallel, produces a reference solution end-to-end. Ground-truth facts uncovered while writing the reference (specific amounts, dates, IDs, root-cause events, seeded inconsistencies) are thenback-injectedinto the source files as verifiable anchors, so that a correct trajectory must recover them exactly rather than approximating them.(iii) Evaluation assets.Each task ships with a Pytest suite, a weighted grade() function with per-dimension rubric, and an LLM-as-Judge prompt—see §3.4. Before a task is admitted to the benchmark, the authors execute it in isolation with≥ 3agents/harnesses; the task

is finalised only if (a) the deterministic evaluators separate correct from incorrect trajectories reliably, (b) every ground-truth fact is discoverable from the provided inputs, and (c) no instruction can be satisfied by string-copying from the source without cross-lingual reasoning. Tasks that fail any check are revised or discarded rather than kept. The complete manifest of tasks, per-task metadata, and construction notes is released with the benchmark.

Each domain contains between11and16tasks (Fig. 2(a,c)). The corpus covers ten languages: English, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, Russian, French, Spanish, German, and Arabic. Coverage is deliberatelytrilingual by construction: instruction, source materials, and expected output are drawn from potentially different languages, so cross-lingual transfer is exercised throughout the trajectory rather than at a single translation step. Concretely,59of67tasks (88%) involve three or more distinct languages across these three roles. Individual language coverage ranges from English (touched by66tasks, mostly as an instruction or output language) to Arabic (1task); Chinese, Korean, Japanese, and Vietnamese each appear in21–51tasks (Fig. 2(b)). Each task instance provides an instruction, a heterogeneous input bundle—documents, tables, contracts, receipts, system logs, localization resources, and business records, with an average of9.3input files per task—executable evaluation scripts where applicable, and a structured reference specification. Instead of

a single reference answer, tasks are scored against fine-grained criteria that capture structural correctness, functional validity, and output quality. On average each task specifies3.9output artefacts (min.2, max.9; total262). The benchmark is extensible: new tasks can be added without modifying the evaluation framework.

PolyWorkBench evaluates task completion along three complementary axes: structural grading, executable verification, and semantic assessment. Each axis targets a failure mode that the others cannot detect on their own. Grademeasures task completion via task-specific structural rules. Each task defines fine-grained criteria for the components of the expected output, allowing partial credit on partially completed solutions while remaining interpretable across heterogeneous artefact types. Pytestevaluates functional correctness on tasks with executable outputs, using automatically executed test 5

Generated outputs are evaluated through three complementary components: structural grading (Grade), executable verification (Pytest), and semantic assessment (LLM-as-Judge). The overall benchmark score is computed from the task-level evaluations. suites. It verifies objective properties—file formats, numerical correctness, schema validity, API outputs, program behaviour—whenever deterministic verification is possible. LLM-as-Judgecovers dimensions that rule-based scoring cannot capture, including coherence, completeness, faithfulness to the task instruction, and overall output quality, evaluated under standardised prompts. Structural grading anchors adherence to the specification, executable tests verify functional correctness, and the judge captures semantic quality beyond deterministic evaluation.

The primary leaderboard metric is Pass@1, the average Grade across all67tasks under a single decoding sample. Grade is chosen as the ranking signal because it directly reflects overall task completion quality across heterogeneous workplace scenarios and admits partial credit on complex outputs. Alongside Grade we report per-task Pytest pass rate and LLM-as-Judge score in[0,1]where applicable. Leaderboard entries additionally record the number of runsnruns; entries with nruns ≥ 2report Pass@3, computed as the best-of-k Grade averaged over tasks. Future releases will further report Pass3 to characterise the stability of autonomous agents under stochastic decoding.

We evaluate a diverse collection of proprietary and open-weight LLMs on all67tasks of PolyWorkBench under a unified evaluation pipeline. To reduce implementation-specific variance, every model is executed inside one of four standardized agent harnesses, each providing a consistent interface for tool invocation, environment interaction, and result collection:ClaudeCode,OpenClaw,Hermes, andCodex. All harnesses share the same task inputs, timeout budget (1,800seconds per task), and evaluation protocol; only the agent scaffolding differs. Following Section 3.4, the primary metric isPass@1, defined as the averageGradescore over all67tasks in a single run. Second, the heatmap shows a systematic Commerce dip: strong all-around models such as DeepSeek-v4-Flash/ClaudeCode and Qwen3.6-27B/ClaudeCode retain0.85–0.90on Knowledge, Legal, and Manufacturing but collapse to0.63and0 .50on Commerce. Commerce tasks in PolyWorkBench mix numerical reconciliation, structured spreadsheet output, cross-currency arithmetic, and strict schema constraints; the pattern suggests that current agents are weakest at long-horizon workflows in which a single arithmetic or schema mistake voids the entire deliverable, whereas Knowledge or Legal tasks tolerate partial correctness through structural credit. This asymmetry has practical consequences: overall Pass@1 misrepresents the reliability of an agent for enterprise workflows that require strict end-to-end correctness. Concrete examples of this failure mode, including tasks that break specifically at the arithmetic verification step, are catalogued in Appendix A.1. Multilingual generalization.The right panel of Figure 4 shows per-language mean Grade for the same18 entries. Strong closed-source models such as Opus 4.8/ClaudeCode remain balanced across the ten languages

(0.82–0.96), whereas mid-tier models degrade sharply on Russian, Spanish, and German. The gap between the best and worst per-language mean of a fixed model can exceed30Grade points – larger than the overall Pass@1 differences between adjacent leaderboard rows – so language variation is not simply an additive shift on top of monolingual capability but a genuine axis of failure. Chinese, Vietnamese, and Japanese are relatively easy across the board, most likely because those tasks over-index on structured-output artefacts whose grading is easier to satisfy once the entities are read correctly. Two failure modes recur inside the low-language cells. Some are pure comprehension errors, in which the agent misreads figures or entities in the source language and never recovers. Others are cross-lingual coordination errors, in which comprehension is correct but the agent fails to keep source-language content and target-language output aligned across a multi-step trajectory, so the final artefact drifts even though every intermediate step looked plausible. Extended per-language statistics, including per-domain breakdowns and low-resource cases, are given in Appendix A.2. 8

Bars for a given model span0–24Pass@1 points; ClaudeCode is best or tied-best whenever it is available, but the ordering of the remaining harnesses is not model-invariant. and DeepSeek-v4-Flash spans0 .099across four harnesses (0.796ClaudeCode → 0.698Hermes). In every case, ClaudeCode is either the best or tied-best harness for the model, but the ordering of the remaining three harnesses is not stable across models: Codex beats Hermes for DeepSeek-v4-Flash but is untested for the Claude family, and Hermes is competitive with OpenClaw only for Qwen models. In this paper, we introduce PolyWorkBench, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on realistic long-horizon workflows spanning five representative domains. PolyWorkBench comprises 67 carefully designed tasks that require multilingual understanding, heterogeneous document processing, structured output generation, and multi-step tool interaction. To provide reliable and comprehensive assessment, we develop a unified evaluation framework that integrates task-specific grading, executable verification, and LLM-based semantic judgment. Extensive experiments on representative proprietary and open-weight models demonstrate that multilingual long-horizon workflows remain challenging for current LLM agents. Our analysis further reveals substantial variation across task domains and languages, underscoring the importance of evaluating multilingual agents beyond isolated reasoning or single-domain settings. We hope PolyWorkBench will provide a practical benchmark for measuring progress toward more capable and reliable multilingual LLM agents. As future work, we plan to continuously expand the benchmark with additional languages, domains, and evolving real-world workflows, enabling long-term evaluation as multilingual agent capabilities continue to advance. 10

This appendix collects extended results moved out of Section 4 for space. The three subsections mirror the three references in the main text: per-domain failure cases, extended per-language statistics, and illustrative Judge disagreement cases. All numbers are computed from the same pool of1,206(entry, task) observations analysed in the main body.

Section 4 noted that Commerce is the systematic weakness of most model×harness pairs in the mid-tier of the leaderboard. Table 2 lists the eight Commerce tasks on which the largest number of evaluated agents scored < 0.4Grade, together with the mean Grade over the failing subset. The pattern is consistent: five of the eight tasks are failed by≥ 15of the18evaluated agents. Manual inspection shows that these tasks share the same structural profile – multi-step numerical reconciliation, currency conversion, or strict spreadsheet schemas – in which a single arithmetic or format error voids the entire deliverable and yields a near-zero Grade. In contrast, Knowledge or Legal tasks tolerate partial correctness through structural credit, so the same class of local error only shaves a few points off Grade rather than collapsing it to zero. This asymmetry is the mechanical driver of the Commerce dip visible in Figure 4 (a). Beyond the Commerce cluster, three cross-domain observations are worth recording. (i) Legal is the domain with the widest Pass@1 spread across models: Opus 4.8/ClaudeCode reaches0.951but the median entry sits at0 .711, indicating that legal analysis remains a differentiator between frontier and open-weight agents. blocks.text: Section 4 argued that the low Grade–Judge correlation is not evidence of a broken metric, but rather evidence that the Judge measures a different quality axis. Table 4 provides concrete cases from the “high Grade + Pytest, near-zero Judge” quadrant of the disagreement plot. All entries have Pytest≥ 0.9and Grade ≥ 0.85, yet Judge is at most0.02. The tasks that appear in this quadrant fall into three genres: (i) long-form generative outputs where structural correctness is decoupled from writing quality (KNW-11 crosslingual factcheck, LEG-14 patent prior art, KNW-06 fr policy brief); (ii) locale/persona artefacts where a template can be filled correctly but still read as unnatural to the Judge (LOC-09 ko chatbot persona, LOC-02 vi marketing campaign, LOC-06 zh video subtitles); and (iii) multi-locale release notes where the Judge penalises inconsistency across localised strings that Grade does not check (LOC-10 multi-locale release). All three genres share the property that the deterministic evaluators sign off on the artefact but a fluent reader would find it deficient. This is exactly the class of failure that PolyWorkBench keeps the Judge component to detect; the low Pearson correlation reflects the design goal, not a metric failure. 14

For completeness we also note the opposite direction:70(entry, task) pairs haveGrade≤ 0.2but Judge≥ 0.8. Manual inspection shows that these are almost entirely Commerce tasks (COM-01, COM-07, COM-10) where the agent produced a well-written narrative or explanation that the Judge found convincing, but failed the deterministic numerical or schema check that Grade and Pytest enforce. This is the mirror image of the pattern in Table 4: Judge rewards fluent explanation, Grade requires the artefact to be numerically correct, and neither of them alone captures both. The joint reporting of all three metrics is therefore the intended semantics of the benchmark rather than a redundancy to be simplified away. 15
